tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what Book Scanner does and how to run it locally. The guide describes the full workflow — photograph book pages, extract text via OCR, generate speech with ElevenLabs, then play the result back as an audiobook. It also covers every service needed for local development: PostgreSQL, MinIO (S3-compatible storage), and a Google Cloud Vision key.

tour.title: Local Dev Infrastructure
tour.description: The docker-compose file spins up the two external services the API depends on: PostgreSQL for relational data and MinIO for object storage. Before any code runs, these containers must be healthy — understanding them up front explains why the app has separate database and storage abstractions rather than storing files in the database.

tour.title: Data Model
tour.description: The Prisma schema is the canonical map of every entity in the system. A User owns many Projects; each Project contains ordered PageImages (the photos); each PageImage has TextRegions (the rectangles a user draws to mark OCR areas); OCR produces Scenes (text segments); and each Scene gets an AudioTrack (the synthesized speech file). Reading this schema once gives you the vocabulary used in every route and mobile screen throughout the tour.

tour.title: Backend Entry Point
tour.description: The API is a two-file boot sequence: index.ts simply starts the HTTP listener, while app.ts does all the real wiring — it registers every route module, attaches the global error handler, and exports the configured Express instance for both the server and the test suite. With a fan-out of 28, app.ts is the most important single file in the backend: understanding it shows you every surface the API exposes.

tour.title: Authentication Layer
tour.description: Every protected API route passes through two collaborating modules. jwt.ts mints and verifies three token types — access tokens (short-lived), refresh tokens (long-lived), and asset tokens (single-use, for signing audio/image URLs). The auth middleware uses jwt.ts to validate the Bearer header on incoming requests and attach the decoded user to req. These two files are referenced by 16 and 11 other files respectively, making them the most cross-cutting security concern in the backend.

tour.title: Database Client
tour.description: db.ts exports a single Prisma client singleton shared across every route handler and library module — 26 files import it, making it the second most depended-upon file in the whole codebase. The singleton pattern prevents connection exhaustion: creating a new Prisma client per request would open a new connection pool each time, but the singleton reuses the same pool across the entire server lifetime.

tour.title: Mobile App Shell
tour.description: On the mobile side, the root _layout.tsx bootstraps the Expo Router tree: it loads custom fonts, wraps the entire app in AuthProvider and ToastProvider, and sets up the navigation stack. One level deeper, the authenticated shell layout guards every screen behind an auth check — if the auth context reports no session, the user is redirected to the login flow before any project data is fetched.

tour.title: Auth Context & API Client
tour.description: auth-context.tsx is the mobile counterpart to the backend's JWT middleware: it manages the logged-in user state globally, persists tokens to secure storage, and exposes login/logout/register actions to every screen. api.ts is the other pillar — a centralized singleton that wraps every backend endpoint in a typed function, adding the Authorization header automatically. With a fan-in of 31, api.ts is the single most depended-upon file in the entire codebase.

tour.title: Creating a Project
tour.description: The audiobook creation journey begins with two wizard screens. new/index.tsx collects the book title, language, narrator voice, and optional jingle preference, then calls the API to create the Project record. new/images.tsx is where the user photographs or picks their book pages — it orchestrates the upload pipeline, lets the user draw OCR text regions on each image, and then fires off the OCR and audio generation jobs. On the backend, the projects route and images route handle the corresponding REST calls and persist PageImage records with sharp-generated thumbnails.

tour.title: Object Storage
tour.description: storage.ts sits between every route that handles files and the underlying MinIO/S3 bucket. It auto-creates the bucket on first use and exposes typed helpers for upload, download, delete, and existence checks. This abstraction is why switching from MinIO to AWS S3 in production requires changing only a single file — the bucket name and endpoint credentials — while all nine route handlers that depend on storage.ts remain untouched.

tour.title: OCR: Photo to Text
tour.description: OCR is the first transformation in the audiobook pipeline. The scenes route accepts a trigger request and queues background OCR jobs; the ocr route exposes per-scene and batch-project recognition endpoints. The ocr library calls Google Cloud Vision's batch annotation API, passing each page image path together with the TextRegion rectangles the user drew in the wizard — Vision returns the raw text, which is stored as Scene records in the database. Back on mobile, new/review.tsx polls until all scenes finish processing, then lets the user edit the extracted text before audio generation begins.

tour.title: TTS: Text to Audio
tour.description: Once the user approves the OCR transcript, audio generation begins. The audio route accepts per-scene TTS requests; tts.ts calls the ElevenLabs API with the scene text and the voice profile chosen during project creation, then stores the resulting MP3 in MinIO via storage.ts and records the AudioTrack in the database. A mock implementation is available when no ElevenLabs key is configured, enabling full offline development. The images wizard's waitForGeneratedAudio helper polls the API until every AudioTrack is ready before navigating the user forward.

tour.title: Project Hub Screen
tour.description: The project detail screen (projects/[id]/index.tsx) is the central hub after creation: it displays the project cover and metadata, embeds an audio player with scene-by-scene navigation, and exposes action buttons to edit scenes, change voices, or share the audiobook. It also triggers audio generation from here when the user wants to regenerate tracks. Understanding this screen connects everything built so far — projects, scenes, audio tracks, and the player — into one user-facing view.

tour.title: Audiobook Player
tour.description: player.tsx is the payoff: the full audiobook playback screen that combines the expo-av audio engine, scene transcript display, offline caching, and playback controls. It fetches signed asset URLs (generated by jwt.ts's short-lived asset tokens) so the audio stream is authenticated without exposing permanent storage URLs. SceneTranscriptBox syncs the transcript text scroll position to the audio playback time, giving the user a karaoke-style reading experience.

tour.title: AudioFlow Design System
tour.description: The visual language of every screen in the tour is defined in two files: audioflow-tokens.ts declares the complete design token map — colors, spacing, typography, and radii — while audioflow.tsx is the component library built on top of those tokens, exporting 20+ primitives like Screen, Card, Button, and progress indicators. With a fan-in of 23, audioflow.tsx is the third most imported file in the codebase. Centralizing tokens here means a brand color change requires editing one line rather than hunting through dozens of StyleSheet objects.
